title: Worsening headache after a fall in a 72-year-old man on apixaban
desc: The candidate is a junior doctor in a rural ED. Harold Brennan, 72, has had three days of a slowly worsening headache. They take a focused history, which brings out a minor fall five days earlier in which he hit the right side of his head, and the fact that he takes apixaban. They then do a focused examination. In Part 2 they interpret his observations, which show early neurological deterioration, his bloods and a non-contrast CT brain. They diagnose a right subdural haematoma with midline shift, reverse the anticoagulant, arrange urgent neurosurgical referral and retrieval, address the cause of the fall, and answer his fear that he has a brain tumour.
focus: Recognising a subdural haematoma after minor head trauma in an anticoagulated older adult: the history, interpreting the CT, reversing the anticoagulant and getting him to neurosurgery
diagnosis: Right subdural haematoma with midline shift
stem: You are a junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a rural hospital. Harold Brennan, a 72-year-old retired accountant, has come in with a headache. He is sitting on a trolley in a cubicle. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Brennan and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, blood results and CT brain report, and ask you four questions: an ISBAR handover including your interpretation, your diagnosis and differentials, your management, and a question from Harold (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Harold Brennan, 72, a retired accountant. You are precise and polite, a little embarrassed to be making a fuss, and you play down the fall because you did not think it mattered. Every so often you rub the right side of your head. You are fully alert and oriented throughout Part 1. Give the history below only when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've been having a headache lately and it's been getting worse."

The headache (give only when asked)

  • Onset: it started 3 days ago and came on slowly. At first you ignored it, thinking rest would fix it.
  • Site: "It's sort of all over, but more on the right side."
  • Character: a dull ache.
  • Severity: 5/10 at the start, 7/10 now.
  • Course: it has got steadily worse. Nothing makes it better or worse.
  • Before: you have never had a headache like this.
  • Effect: "It's annoying and distracting. It's getting in the way of everything."

The fall (give only if asked about falls, injuries or knocks to the head)

  • Five days ago you slipped on the last step at home and hit the right side of your head on the wall.
  • You did not black out. There was no bleeding and no cut. You felt better after a rest, so you did not see anyone. "I didn't think it was serious."
  • If asked why you fell: you were in your socks and slipped. You did not feel dizzy, faint or light-headed beforehand, had no racing heart, and your eyesight was fine. You remember the whole thing.
  • You had no symptoms afterwards apart from a sore spot on your head.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No sudden "thunderclap" or worst-ever headache.
  • No drowsiness, no episodes of being hard to wake or "not with it", and no confusion. Your wife has not noticed anything different.
  • No vomiting or nausea. No fits.
  • No weakness, numbness or pins and needles. No slurred speech or drooping face. No change in balance or walking.
  • No blurred or double vision. No red or painful eye. No halos around lights.
  • No fever, neck stiffness, discomfort with bright lights or rash.
  • Not worse in the morning or when lying down, coughing or straining.
  • No scalp tenderness when combing your hair (apart from the sore spot where you hit your head) and no jaw pain when chewing.
  • No weight loss, night sweats or loss of appetite.
  • No aura or flashing lights. No band-like tightness, no watery eye or runny nose on one side.

Past medical history

  • Mild high blood pressure, managed with diet and walking. No tablets for it.
  • Atrial fibrillation ("an irregular heartbeat"), diagnosed some years ago.
  • Keyhole gallbladder removal at age 45.
  • Immunisations are up to date.

Medications and allergies

  • Apixaban 5 mg twice a day ("my blood thinner"). You never miss a dose. Last dose: 8 o'clock this morning.
  • No aspirin, anti-inflammatories or other medicines.
  • Allergy: penicillin (rash).

Family history

  • Your mother died of a heart attack at 81.
  • Your father died of lung cancer at 60.

Social history

  • Ex-smoker: about 10 pack-years, between the ages of 25 and 40.
  • A glass of wine with dinner on weekends. No other drugs.
  • You live with your wife. She is in the waiting room.
  • You walk for 15 minutes every morning and eat balanced, home-cooked meals.
  • No particular stress. You play lawn bowls with friends.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "No idea!" You have not linked the headache to the fall.
  • Concerns: "Do I have brain cancer?" (your father died of cancer).
  • Expectations: you want to know what is going on.

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • Gives the observations and a bedside glucose when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If the candidate asks for a collateral history, the nurse says your wife reports that you have been yourself, with no confusion or drowsiness that she has noticed.
  • If the candidate orders a cannula, bloods, a CT brain, neurological observations or analgesia, says "I'll get that started." If a drug is ordered without a dose or route, asks "What dose and route would you like?"
  • If Prothrombinex-VF is ordered, accept 25 to 50 units/kg IV (2000 to 4000 units for his 80 kg), or "as per local protocol".
  • If the candidate orders an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen, asks once: "He's on apixaban. Do you still want that?"
  • If paracetamol is given, Harold says it takes the edge off a little.
  • If the candidate asks for blood or CT results, says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: alert, comfortable at rest, rubbing the right side of his head. Weight 80 kg.
  • Observations: RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 158/86, HR 84 irregularly irregular, temperature 36.8 °C, CRT 2 seconds, pain 7/10. Bedside glucose 6.2 mmol/L.
  • Conscious state: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). Oriented to time, place and person. Short cognitive screen normal if done.
  • Pupils: 3 mm, equal and reactive to light.
  • Head and scalp: tender over the right parietal area. No laceration, no boggy swelling and no visible bruising. No periorbital or mastoid (Battle's) bruising. No blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears. Tympanic membranes normal.
  • Neck: no cervical spine tenderness, full range of movement. No neck stiffness. Kernig's sign negative.
  • Cranial nerves: visual acuity normal with his glasses. Visual fields full. Fundoscopy: sharp discs, no papilloedema. Eye movements full with no nystagmus or double vision. Face symmetrical. Speech normal.
  • Limbs: tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. No pronator drift. Plantars flexor. Finger-nose and heel-shin normal.
  • Gait: normal, Romberg's test negative.
  • Eyes and temporal arteries: eyes white and not tender. Temporal arteries soft, non-tender and pulsatile.
  • Skin: no rash.
  • Cardiovascular: pulse 84, irregularly irregular. Heart sounds dual with no murmur. Postural BP if asked: lying 158/86, standing 152/84, no symptoms.
  • Respiratory and abdomen: chest clear. Abdomen soft, with healed laparoscopic port scars.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Harold's identity and gains consent before examining.
Uses plain language and acknowledges his worry about brain cancer with empathy, without false reassurance (for example, says a scan is needed to find the cause).
History
Characterises the headache:
check.d: Critical core: establishes that the headache is new and progressively worsening.

kids.x: Onset 3 days ago, slow; ignored at first; never had one like it before
Diffuse but more on the right; dull
Annoying and distracting, affecting daily life

check.x: Asks about falls or head injury and elicits the fall: 5 days ago, slipped on the last step, hit the right side of his head on the wall, no loss of consciousness, no wound, did not seek help.
Asks what caused the fall: slipped in socks; no dizziness, palpitations, visual problem or blackout.

Asks about features of neurological deterioration or raised intracranial pressure: drowsiness or fluctuating consciousness, confusion, vomiting, seizures, weakness or numbness, speech change, balance or gait change, and visual change (all negative).
check.d: Award if the candidate asks about drowsiness or fluctuating consciousness, confusion, vomiting and focal weakness at a minimum.

check.x: Screens for at least six other causes, including two haemorrhagic and two other secondary causes:
check.d: Full marks for 6 or more causes screened, including 2 haemorrhagic and 2 other secondary causes.

kids.x: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: thunderclap or worst-ever onset
Extradural haemorrhage: loss of consciousness after the fall with a lucid interval
Stroke or TIA: sudden onset of symptoms, facial droop
Meningitis or encephalitis: fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, rash
Tumour or systemic illness: worse in the morning or on coughing or lying, weight loss, night sweats
Temporal arteritis (scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss) or acute glaucoma (red painful eye, halos)
Primary headache: migraine (aura, nausea), tension-type (band-like) or cluster (watery eye, runny nose)

check.x: Identifies the anticoagulant: apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, taken reliably, with the last dose at 08:00 today, and no aspirin or NSAIDs.
Takes the past medical history: mild hypertension (not medicated), atrial fibrillation, laparoscopic cholecystectomy at 45, immunisations up to date.
Asks about allergies: penicillin (rash).

Takes a brief family history (mother MI at 81, father lung cancer at 60) and social history (ex-smoker of about 10 pack-years from age 25 to 40, weekend wine, no drugs, lives with his wife, walks daily, lawn bowls).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: no idea of the cause, fear of brain cancer, and wanting to know what is going on.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a bedside glucose, and notes BP 158/86, an irregularly irregular HR of 84 (known AF), normal temperature and glucose 6.2 mmol/L.
Assesses conscious state by GCS component (E4 V5 M6 = 15) and checks that the pupils are equal and reactive.

Inspects and palpates the head: right parietal tenderness with no laceration or swelling. Looks for signs of a base of skull fracture (periorbital or mastoid bruising, CSF leak, haemotympanum) and checks the cervical spine.
Performs a focused neurological examination and finds no focal deficit:

kids.x: Cranial nerves, including visual fields and fundoscopy (no papilloedema)
Limbs: tone, power, reflexes, sensation and pronator drift

check.x: Examines for mimics: meningism and rash, temporal arteries, and the eyes (red or tender eye). All normal.
Looks for a cause of the fall: pulse rhythm (irregularly irregular), heart sounds, and lying and standing BP (no postural drop).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all in the white zone until 15:00, when he rouses only to voice (yellow zone), GCS falls from 15 to 14, headache is worse and the nurse is concerned. Identifies this as neurological deterioration needing a senior doctor at the bedside now.
Interprets the CT brain:

kids.x: A crescent-shaped collection over the right convexity that crosses suture lines is subdural, not extradural (lentiform, limited by sutures). Mixed density fits acute and subacute blood
Mass effect: right sulcal effacement, compression of the right lateral ventricle and 8 mm leftward midline shift, with a 15 mm thick haematoma, so it needs neurosurgery. No fracture or other bleed

check.x: Interprets the bloods: Hb and platelets normal. States that a near-normal INR and APTT do not exclude apixaban effect: the last dose was at 08:00 and renal function is adequate (eGFR 68). Normal sodium and glucose rule out hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia as causes of the new drowsiness. Group and screen is done.

Gives the diagnosis as a right subdural haematoma with mass effect and midline shift after minor head trauma in a patient on apixaban, with supporting features (the fall, a progressive headache worse on the right, anticoagulation, the CT).
Names at least three differentials, each with a feature against it, from: extradural haematoma, subarachnoid haemorrhage, intracranial tumour, temporal arteritis and tension-type headache.
Management

In Part 1, recognises a high-risk head injury (older, anticoagulated, progressive headache after a fall). Orders an urgent non-contrast CT brain, withholds apixaban, orders bloods (FBC, coagulation, UEC, group and screen) and neurological observations, and informs a senior.
check.d: Part 1 item. Credit only if the CT is requested during Part 1.

check.x: Resuscitates and monitors: DRSABCD, senior ED doctor to the bedside, neurological observations (GCS and pupils) every 15 minutes, head of the bed up 30 degrees, nil by mouth, and avoids hypoxia and hypotension.
check.d: Critical core: senior doctor to the bedside and neurological observations (GCS and pupils) every 15 minutes; head-up, nil by mouth and avoiding hypoxia and hypotension are expected but not individually required.

check.x: Stops and reverses the anticoagulant:

kids.x: Reverses now with prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF) or andexanet alfa where available, per local protocol with haematology advice. Either agent earns the mark. Does not use vitamin K or FFP as the reversal agent (fail this item only if vitamin K or FFP is given instead of a factor Xa reversal strategy).
kids.d: Accept a reasonable dose per protocol (Prothrombinex-VF 25 to 50 units/kg IV); do not require a specific dose.

check.x: Makes an urgent neurosurgical referral to the tertiary centre and arranges retrieval from the rural ED, with images sent and retrieval or ICU advice. Plans airway protection if GCS falls to 8 or less or the airway is at risk.
Gives paracetamol 1 g IV 6-hourly (maximum 4 g per day) while nil by mouth, and no NSAIDs.
check.d: Accept oral paracetamol only if it was given in Part 1 before he was made nil by mouth.

check.x: Explains to Harold in plain words that this is bleeding on the surface of the brain from the fall, made worse by the blood thinner, and not a cancer, and that he needs transfer and probably an operation. Offers to involve his wife.
Safety netting

Sets nurse escalation triggers while awaiting transfer: any further fall in GCS or harder to rouse, confusion, unequal or sluggish pupils, new weakness or speech change, a seizure, vomiting or worsening headache, and a slowing HR with rising BP. States that any further fall in GCS of 2 or more points, or a response only to pain, is a rapid response call.
check.d: Critical core: names at least four specific triggers, including a fall in GCS or harder to rouse and a pupil change, and says the doctor is called immediately. The rapid response threshold is expected but not individually required.

check.x: Tells Harold and his wife what to report straight away (worse headache, drowsiness, confusion, vomiting, weakness or a fit) and that the bleed can recur over weeks.

Arranges follow-up: neurosurgical follow-up with repeat imaging and no driving until cleared, a falls work-up (ECG, postural BP, vision, footwear, home) and a specialist decision on restarting anticoagulation.
check.d: Award if the candidate names at least two of: neurosurgical follow-up with repeat imaging and no driving until cleared; a falls assessment; a specialist decision on restarting anticoagulation.

part2.lead: It is now 15:10. Here are Harold's observations since he arrived, his blood results and the CT brain report.
part2.patient:
For the fourth question, ask this once: "So do I have brain cancer?" If the candidate says it is not cancer but does not mention surgery, add: "Will I need an operation?"

Harold is now a little sleepy but still answers sensibly. If the candidate uses jargon ("subdural", "haematoma", "midline shift", "reversal"), ask "What does that mean?" If they explain clearly, say: "Right. Can someone tell my wife, please?"

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Room air throughout. GCS and pupils recorded with each set.
handover.model:
• Read: at 13:10 and 14:15 every value is in the white zone: RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air, systolic BP 158 to 162, HR 80 to 84 irregular (known AF), temperature 36.8 °C, alert, GCS 15, pupils equal. At 15:00 he rouses only to voice (yellow zone), GCS has fallen from 15 to 14 (E3 V5 M6), headache is 8/10, BP 164/88 and HR 82 in AF are unchanged, and the nurse is concerned.
  • Meaning: early neurological deterioration. The haematoma is expanding or intracranial pressure is rising. There is no Cushing response yet; watch for bradycardia with rising BP and an irregular breathing pattern, a late sign of herniation.
  • Changes: the yellow zone value and staff concern are Clinical Review criteria. With an SDH and midline shift he needs a senior doctor at the bedside now, neurological observations every 15 minutes, reversal now, and expedited transfer. Any further fall in GCS of 2 or more points, or a response only to pain, is a rapid response call.

Back from CT. GCS 15, pupils 3 mm equal and reactive

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 13:25 at cannulation. Lab comment: patient reports last apixaban dose at 08:00 today; apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa level not available on site.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 141 and platelets 224, both normal. INR 1.2 (upper limit), APTT 33 and fibrinogen normal. Sodium 138, potassium 4.3, urea 7.2, creatinine 96 (eGFR 68, CrCl about 70 mL/min) and glucose 6.4, all normal. Blood group O Rh(D) positive, antibody screen negative.
  • Meaning: no thrombocytopenia or anaemia. The near-normal INR and APTT do not mean apixaban has worn off: the last dose was at 08:00 and his renal clearance is adequate, so he should be treated as fully anticoagulated. Normal sodium and glucose rule out hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia as causes of the new drowsiness.
  • Changes: reverse the anticoagulant now without waiting for a drug level. Group and screen is ready for theatre. Renal function is the baseline.

handover.label: CT brain report
handover.result:
Examination: CT brain, non-contrast, 13:50.

Clinical details: 72-year-old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Fall 5 days ago striking the right side of the head, no loss of consciousness. Three days of progressive headache. GCS 15, no focal deficit. ?Intracranial haemorrhage.

Findings:

  • Extra-axial spaces: crescent-shaped collection in the subdural space over the right cerebral convexity, extending from the frontal to the occipital region and not limited by the suture lines. Mixed density, predominantly hyperdense with isodense components. Maximal thickness 15 mm. No extradural collection. No subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • Mass effect: effacement of the right cerebral sulci compared with the left. Partial effacement of the right lateral ventricle. Midline shift of 8 mm to the left at the level of the septum pellucidum. Basal cisterns patent. No uncal or tonsillar herniation. No hydrocephalus.
  • Brain parenchyma: no intraparenchymal haemorrhage or contusion. No mass lesion. Age-appropriate involutional change.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no skull fracture. Paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells clear.

Conclusion: right convexity subdural haematoma of mixed density (acute and subacute components), maximal thickness 15 mm, with mass effect and 8 mm leftward midline shift. No skull fracture or other intracranial haemorrhage. Urgent neurosurgical discussion recommended.
handover.model:
• Read: a non-contrast CT. There is an extra-axial collection over the right convexity that is crescent-shaped and crosses the suture lines, so it is subdural. An extradural collection is lentiform and limited by the sutures. Its mixed density means acute and subacute blood. Mass effect: right sulcal effacement, compression of the right lateral ventricle, 8 mm midline shift, cisterns still patent. No fracture, contusion, subarachnoid blood or mass.
  • Meaning: a large right subdural haematoma from the fall 5 days ago, expanding on apixaban. It explains the progressive right-sided headache and the new drowsiness. There is no tumour.
  • Changes: a thickness over 10 mm and a midline shift over 5 mm meet the threshold for surgical evacuation. He needs urgent neurosurgical referral and transfer from this rural ED, and anticoagulant reversal now.

ask: You are now calling the neurosurgical registrar at the tertiary referral hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Harold Brennan, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Harold now, here in this rural emergency department, including what you will ask the nurse to escalate while he waits for retrieval.
Harold asks you, "So do I have brain cancer?" Please answer him, including what he and his wife should watch for and the follow-up he will need.

• Identify: self, junior doctor at the rural ED; Harold Brennan, 72.
  • Situation: right subdural haematoma with 8 mm midline shift on apixaban; GCS fell from 15 to 14 at 15:00.
  • Background: fall 5 days ago hitting the right side of his head, no LOC; 3 days of progressive headache; AF on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, last dose 08:00; mild hypertension; penicillin allergy.
  • Assessment: now rousable to voice, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6), pupils equal, BP 164/88, HR 82 in AF; no focal deficit. CT: mixed-density right SDH, 15 mm, sulcal effacement, 8 mm shift, no fracture. Hb and platelets normal; INR 1.2 does not exclude apixaban effect; eGFR 68; Na 138 and glucose 6.4 normal, so not a metabolic cause of the drowsiness; group and screen done.
  • Recommendation: please accept for urgent evacuation; reversal being given with haematology advice; arranging retrieval; images sent; any advice while he waits.

Right subdural haematoma with mass effect, anticoagulant-associated: minor fall hitting the right side of his head, 3 days of progressive right-sided headache, apixaban, now drowsier; crescentic mixed-density collection crossing sutures with 8 mm shift.

  • Extradural haematoma: for: head injury; against: no LOC or lucid interval, no fracture, and the collection is crescentic and crosses sutures.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: against: gradual onset, no thunderclap or meningism, no subarachnoid blood on CT.
  • Intracranial tumour: for: new progressive headache at 72, his fear; against: clear trauma, no mass on CT.
  • Temporal arteritis or tension-type headache: against: no scalp or jaw symptoms; new, progressive and after trauma.

1. DRSABCD: senior ED doctor to the bedside now; neurological observations every 15 minutes; head up 30 degrees; nil by mouth; avoid hypoxia and hypotension.
  2. Stop apixaban and reverse now: Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV (4000 units for 80 kg), or per local protocol, with haematology advice; andexanet alfa where available and per local protocol. Vitamin K does not reverse apixaban.
  3. Urgent neurosurgical referral: 15 mm with 8 mm shift meets the threshold for evacuation; retrieval to the tertiary centre with images sent; retrieval or ICU advice; intubate if GCS is 8 or less or the airway is at risk.
  4. Paracetamol 1 g IV 6-hourly (maximum 4 g/day) while nil by mouth; no NSAIDs.
  5. Nurse escalation while awaiting retrieval: call me immediately for any further fall in GCS or harder to rouse, confusion, unequal or sluggish pupils, new weakness or speech change, a seizure, vomiting or worsening headache, or a slowing HR with rising BP; a fall in GCS of 2 or more points or response only to pain is a rapid response call.

• Not cancer: the scan shows a collection of blood on the surface of the brain from the knock 5 days ago. The blood thinner let it keep slowly bleeding, which is why the headache crept up.
  • Now: medicine to undo the blood thinner, transfer to a neurosurgical hospital, and very likely an operation to drain the blood; his wife will be told.
  • Tell the staff straight away about: worse headache, drowsiness, confusion, vomiting, weakness or a fit; the bleed can come back over weeks.
  • Follow-up: neurosurgery and a repeat scan, no driving until cleared; a falls check; specialists decide on restarting the blood thinner.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and glucose when asked, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The fall comes out only if the candidate asks about falls, injuries or knocks to the head. The time of the last apixaban dose comes out only if asked. Harold stays alert, with GCS 15, throughout Part 1. If the candidate asks for blood or CT results, say they come in Part 2. Item 29 is credited only if the CT is requested in Part 1. If apixaban is withheld or reversal is ordered in Part 1, credit item 31 when the candidate repeats or confirms it in Part 2. For Prothrombinex-VF, accept 25 to 50 units/kg IV or "as per local protocol".

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. For the fourth, the person playing Harold asks the question in the Part 2 script. The deterioration at 15:00 happens whatever the candidate has done.

A high-performing candidate characterises the headache, then asks directly about trauma and finds the fall. They identify apixaban and the time of the last dose, and screen for drowsiness, vomiting and focal symptoms. They also screen the haemorrhagic and other secondary causes. They check GCS by component, pupils, fundi and a focused neurological examination, and order an urgent CT brain while withholding apixaban. In Part 2 they spot the fall in GCS despite a near-white chart and read the CT systematically (crescent crossing sutures, so subdural, with mass effect). They know a normal INR does not exclude apixaban effect, reverse it, get neurosurgery and retrieval moving, and tell Harold plainly that this is not cancer.

A borderline candidate takes a generic headache history and never asks about trauma or anticoagulation, so treats this as tension headache or tumour. They may call the collection extradural, take reassurance from the INR, give vitamin K, plan admission locally for observation, miss the fall in GCS, or give vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: subdural haematoma after minor head trauma on an anticoagulant

A subdural haematoma (SDH) is venous blood between the dura and the arachnoid, usually from tearing of the bridging veins that cross the subdural space. In older people, cerebral atrophy stretches these veins, so a minor fall or knock is enough. Anticoagulants such as apixaban make bleeding more likely and allow a small bleed to keep expanding. The history is often unremarkable: a trivial fall, no loss of consciousness, and a patient who "felt fine" and did not seek help. Days later a slowly progressive headache follows, which may be one-sided, and sometimes drowsiness, confusion, fluctuating consciousness, gait change or focal weakness. Harold's story fits exactly. The key to this station is asking about trauma and anticoagulants in every older person with a new headache.

Taking the headache history

Characterise the headache, then screen in clusters:

  • Haemorrhage: thunderclap onset (subarachnoid), head injury with loss of consciousness and a lucid interval (extradural), or a minor injury followed by a progressive headache (subdural).
  • Stroke or TIA: sudden focal deficit.
  • Infection: fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, rash, confusion (meningitis, encephalitis).
  • Raised intracranial pressure or tumour: morning or postural headache, worse on coughing, vomiting, weight loss.
  • Over 50: temporal arteritis (scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss) and acute angle-closure glaucoma (red painful eye, halos).
  • Primary headaches: migraine, tension-type and cluster. A first primary headache at 72 is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Always ask about drowsiness, fluctuating consciousness, vomiting, balance and visual change. Collateral from his wife helps.

Interpreting the CT

  • Subdural: crescentic (banana-shaped), follows the convexity and crosses suture lines, but not the midline (it is limited by the falx).
  • Extradural: lentiform (lemon-shaped), biconvex and limited by sutures, usually with a skull fracture and middle meningeal artery injury.
  • Density changes with age: acute blood is hyperdense, subacute (days to weeks) becomes isodense and can be subtle, and chronic is hypodense. Mixed density suggests bleeding at different times, such as continued bleeding on an anticoagulant.
  • Mass effect: sulcal effacement compared with the other side, ventricular compression, midline shift and effaced basal cisterns (herniation).

Harold's 15 mm haematoma with 8 mm midline shift is large. The Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines recommend evacuation of an acute SDH thicker than 10 mm or with a midline shift greater than 5 mm, whatever the GCS.

Interpreting the observations and bloods

His RR, SpO2, BP, HR and temperature stay in the white zone, but his level of consciousness moves into the yellow zone (rousable to voice) and his GCS falls by one point. In a patient with an intracranial bleed and midline shift, any fall in conscious state is the key warning, and staff concern is itself a Clinical Review criterion under Between the Flags. Bradycardia with rising BP and an irregular breathing pattern (the Cushing response) is a late sign of herniation. INR and APTT do not reliably measure apixaban activity, so a near-normal result does not show he is safe. The time of the last dose and his renal function matter more.

Management

  • Resuscitate and monitor: DRSABCD, neurological observations (GCS by component and pupils) every 15 minutes while he is deteriorating or awaiting transfer, head up 30 degrees, nil by mouth. Avoid hypoxia and hypotension, which worsen secondary brain injury. Protect the airway if the GCS is 8 or less.
  • Anticoagulant: stop it and reverse it for intracranial haemorrhage. For apixaban and rivaroxaban, give Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV (or per local protocol) with haematology advice; andexanet alfa where available and per local protocol. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not factor Xa inhibitors.
  • Small haematoma in a stable patient: conservative care in a centre that can operate, with neurological observations, repeat CT for expansion, and neurosurgical advice.
  • Large haematoma, midline shift or deterioration (as here): urgent neurosurgical referral. From a rural ED this means early contact with the tertiary neurosurgical team and the state retrieval service, with images sent ahead. Do not wait for him to deteriorate before organising transfer.
  • Supportive care: paracetamol 1 g IV 6-hourly (maximum 4 g/day) while nil by mouth; no NSAIDs. Antiemetics, and treatment of any seizure.
  • Every patient: look for the cause of the fall: vision, arrhythmia (he has AF), postural hypotension, medications, footwear and home hazards. Refer for a falls assessment. Restarting anticoagulation balances his stroke risk from AF against the risk of rebleeding. This decision is made later by neurosurgery and cardiology, not in the ED.

Safety netting and follow-up

While he waits for transfer, nurses escalate any further fall in GCS, confusion, unequal pupils, new weakness or speech change, seizures, vomiting, worsening headache, or a slowing pulse with rising BP. After discharge, Harold and his wife should call 000 for worsening headache, drowsiness, confusion, repeated vomiting, weakness, trouble speaking or a fit, because SDH can recur in the weeks after treatment. Follow-up is with neurosurgery and repeat imaging, his GP, and a falls prevention review, with a planned decision about anticoagulation. He should not drive until cleared under the Austroads standards.
points: In every older person with a new or progressive headache, ask directly about falls or head injury and about anticoagulants. A trivial knock days earlier, with no loss of consciousness, is the typical story for a subdural haematoma.
Subdural haematoma is crescentic and crosses suture lines. Extradural haematoma is lentiform and limited by sutures. Density changes with age: acute hyperdense, subacute isodense, chronic hypodense.

A normal INR and APTT do not exclude apixaban effect. Use the time of the last dose and renal function, and reverse for intracranial haemorrhage: Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV (or per local protocol) with haematology advice; andexanet alfa where available and per local protocol. Vitamin K does not reverse apixaban.
An acute SDH thicker than 10 mm or with more than 5 mm of midline shift needs surgical evacuation. From a rural ED, organise neurosurgical referral and retrieval early.
A falling GCS is the key warning sign even when every vital sign is in the white zone. Watch for the Cushing response (bradycardia with rising BP) as a late sign.
Always address the cause of the fall (vision, arrhythmia, postural BP, footwear, home hazards) and plan the anticoagulation decision with the specialists.
